\title{Reading a 24-Dimensional Lattice Code Without Unfolding It}
\subtitle{A three-section factorisation of the Leech lattice, decoded inside the matrix--vector product}

\author{Pier-Jean Malandrino}
\affiliation{%
  \institution{Scub}
  \city{Bordeaux}
  \country{France}}
\email{pierjean.malandrino@scub.net}

\begin{abstract}
Leech-lattice quantization gives good quality at two bits per weight, but its
codebook holds $1.1\times10^{14}$ points. No lookup table can decode that, so
the kernel we published earlier expanded the representation at load time and
read 4.804 bits per weight from VRAM for 2.000 bits of code.

We keep the lattice and change the codebook. Reordering the 24 coordinates into
three disjoint octads of the Golay code turns the code into a trellis with 64
states per cut, so a lattice point is addressed by an 8-bit state and three
11-bit rows of one shared 16~KiB table, and the lattice's global parity
constraint costs an XOR instead of a stored bit. A block is still 48 bits, the
kernel reads it as stored, and the VRAM rate falls to 2.148 bits per weight.
The price is in the truncation: bounding each section separately fills a
product of three 8-dimensional regions rather than a 24-dimensional ball.

On Qwen3-4B and one L40S the format reads 2.148 bits per weight against 4.179
for a 4-bit AWQ baseline and 4.804 for the layout it replaces. Served, the
model runs at 98.3 tokens per second in 1.39~GB of weights, against 43.4 in
8.04~GB for the f16 checkpoint, at a perplexity of 12.3268 (1.007 times f16)
and an MMLU of 61.11, nine points below it. Results are one model and one card.
\end{abstract}

\keywords{vector quantization, Leech lattice, Golay code, trellis, 2-bit
quantization, GPU kernels, LLM inference}
